name: Lateral ventricle
function: Paired C-shaped CSF cavities within the cerebral hemispheres. The frontal horn lies anterior to the foramen of Monro, the body continues posteriorly under the corpus callosum, and the atrium joins body with occipital and temporal horns. Each lateral ventricle communicates with the third ventricle through its own interventricular foramen. Plexus is present in the body, atrium and temporal horn, not the frontal or occipital horn.

afferent: CSF secretion mainly from its choroid plexus
efferent: Interventricular foramen → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → Magendie/Luschka apertures → subarachnoid space

bloodSupply: The ventricle is a fluid space, not an arterial tissue territory. Adjacent neural walls have region-specific arterial supply; its choroid plexus is supplied mainly by anterior and lateral posterior choroidal arteries. Subependymal/deep veins drain surrounding tissue, not the CSF cavity.

clinical.findings: Blockage at a foramen of Monro can enlarge one or both lateral ventricles; aqueductal blockage usually enlarges both lateral and third ventricles with a relatively normal fourth. Symptoms and transependymal flow depend on pressure and time course.

A clinical syndrome with gait impairment, cognitive difficulty and urinary symptoms associated with ventriculomegaly. The full triad is not required and one normal pressure measurement is not diagnostic; ventricular size alone cannot distinguish it from atrophy.

In premature infants, fragile germinal-matrix vessels near the caudothalamic groove can bleed into the ventricle. Subsequent CSF obstruction and impaired absorption may cause post-haemorrhagic ventricular dilatation.
Mild asymmetry can be a normal variant. Interpretation requires surrounding tissue, obstruction and clinical context, rather than a horn-size rule alone.

name: Frontal horn of the lateral ventricle
synonyms: anterior horn of the lateral ventricle
function: Blind anterior recess of the lateral ventricle, anterior to the foramen of Monro. Its roof/anterior boundary is related to corpus callosum, medial wall to septum pellucidum, lateral wall/floor to caudate head, and inferior medial boundary to callosal rostrum. It contains no choroid plexus and communicates posteriorly with the body.
contextNote: Schematic segment of the committed lateral-ventricular model. The origin and dimensions are display anchors in the atlas frame; segment cut planes and mesh-centroid measurements do not validate boundaries or dimensions in an individual brain. Refer to the complete cast and surrounding anatomical relationships.

afferent: CSF communication with the ventricular body; no local plexus

bloodSupply: No arterial supply to the CSF space itself. Caudate/septal/callosal walls receive their own variable ACA/MCA/deep perforator supply; venous drainage concerns the wall tissue.

clinical.findings: Frontal-horn width can be used in the Evans index (maximum frontal horn width / maximum internal skull width). A value around or above 0.30 is commonly used as a ventriculomegaly screening threshold, but it does not establish hydrocephalus or its cause.
A colloid cyst or other lesion near Monro may obstruct one or both lateral ventricles. Enlargement is upstream, not proven to start exclusively in the frontal horns.
Premature-infant caudothalamic germinal-matrix haemorrhage can extend into the frontal horn/body. Periventricular haemorrhagic infarction is not simply an extension grade of intraventricular blood.

name: Temporal horn of the lateral ventricle
synonyms: inferior horn of the lateral ventricle
function: Inferior horn extends from the atrium inferiorly and then anteriorly into the temporal lobe. Hippocampus and collateral eminence contribute to its floor, with fimbria/choroidal fissure along the medial margin; roof relations include tapetum, caudate tail and stria terminalis. Choroid plexus extends into this horn from the atrium.
contextNote: Schematic segment of the committed lateral-ventricular model. The origin and dimensions are display anchors in the atlas frame; segment cut planes and mesh-centroid measurements do not validate boundaries or dimensions in an individual brain. Refer to the complete cast and surrounding anatomical relationships.

afferent: CSF communication with atrium; secretion from local choroid plexus
efferent: Back through atrium/body to the interventricular foramen; no independent outlet

bloodSupply: The cavity has no intrinsic arterial supply. Temporal-horn choroid plexus receives anterior choroidal and lateral posterior choroidal contributions; adjacent hippocampal/amygdalar tissue has variable PCA, anterior choroidal and other regional supply.

clinical.findings: May be an early sign of hydrocephalus, but may also result from hippocampal or temporal tissue atrophy, a trapped horn or normal asymmetry. It does not by itself distinguish obstruction from ex-vacuo enlargement.
clinical.vascular: CSF obstruction or regional volume loss

clinical.findings: Hippocampal atrophy with altered internal architecture and increased T2/FLAIR signal may be accompanied by ipsilateral temporal-horn and choroidal-fissure enlargement, not narrowing. These secondary signs are not sufficient alone for diagnosis.
Neural tissue or plexus near the horn may infarct; the CSF cavity itself does not infarct. Capsular/visual findings depend on the additional affected structures.
clinical.vascular: Anterior choroidal and overlapping regional branches

name: Occipital horn of the lateral ventricle
synonyms: posterior horn of the lateral ventricle
function: Variable posterior recess extending from the atrium into the occipital lobe. Tapetum forms much of its roof and lateral wall; the medial wall can show a bulb related to forceps major and the calcar avis related to the calcarine sulcus. No choroid plexus extends into the occipital horn proper.

The origin and dimensions are display anchors in the atlas frame; segment cut planes and mesh-centroid measurements do not validate boundaries or dimensions in an individual brain. Refer to the complete cast and surrounding anatomical relationships.

efferent: Blind recess; CSF communicates back through atrium/body to Monro

bloodSupply: No arterial supply to the CSF space. Adjacent occipital and callosal tissue has PCA and variable collateral supply; choroidal arteries supply nearby atrial plexus, not plexus within this horn.

clinical.findings: Size and asymmetry vary substantially, and a horn may be very small or absent. A fixed side preference is not established by this model.

Can accompany white-matter volume loss, developmental abnormalities or hydrocephalus. Colpocephaly describes disproportionate occipital-horn enlargement and is not uniquely synonymous with periventricular leukomalacia.

name: Atrium of the lateral ventricle
function: Confluence of body, occipital horn and temporal horn. The glomus is an expanded tuft of choroid plexus here. Tapetal/callosal fibres and the collateral trigone contribute to surrounding boundaries; exact horn/atrium size varies among individuals.
contextNote: Schematic segment of the committed lateral-ventricular model. The origin and dimensions are display anchors in the atlas frame; segment cut planes and mesh-centroid measurements do not validate boundaries or dimensions in an individual brain. Refer to the complete cast and surrounding anatomical relationships.

afferent: Body, temporal horn and occipital horn communicate here; local plexus secretes CSF
efferent: Through body to the foramen of Monro; temporal/occipital horns are recesses, not separate routes to the aqueduct

bloodSupply: No arterial supply to the cavity. Atrial glomus/plexus is supplied chiefly by lateral posterior choroidal branches with anterior choroidal contributions; neighbouring white matter and wall tissue have their own supply.

clinical.findings: Meningioma and other intraventricular masses may arise here, causing headache or obstruction. Adjacent optic-radiation injury or surgical corridor injury may cause a homonymous field defect.
Calcification and small choroid plexus cysts may be incidental. Imaging appearance and context distinguish these from tumor or obstruction.
Can be part of hydrocephalus or regional tissue loss; a universal atrium-before-frontal-horn sequence or least-white-matter explanation is not established.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010) — pp. 132-137, 155-158, 215-216
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012) — pp. 66-69

name: Choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle
function: Vascular villous tissue projecting into the ventricular body, atrium and temporal horn, absent from the frontal and occipital horns. Choroid epithelium actively secretes much of the CSF and its tight junctions form the blood-CSF barrier; the capillaries themselves are fenestrated. It connects with the third-ventricular plexus near the interventricular foramen.

afferent: Arterial blood through anterior/lateral posterior choroidal branches
efferent: CSF secretion into the lateral ventricle
Choroidal venous drainage into deep veins; venous outflow is distinct from the CSF pathway

bloodSupply: Main lateral-ventricular plexus inflow from anterior choroidal and lateral posterior choroidal arteries, with variable anastomotic contributions. Medial posterior choroidal branches primarily supply third-ventricular plexus. Choroidal veins drain into the deep venous system.

clinical.findings: A plexus tumor may cause hydrocephalus through obstruction, CSF overproduction and/or impaired absorption after bleeding. Lateral-ventricular tumors are commoner in children and fourth-ventricular tumors in adults; location alone does not establish tumor type.
Atrial glomus calcification can be a normal age-related finding; age, symmetry, mass and enhancement determine whether further evaluation is needed.
Normal choroid plexus enhances because its capillaries are fenestrated. Abnormal enhancement may occur with inflammation or tumor, but enhancement alone does not diagnose infection.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010) — pp. 132-137, 155-158, 215-216
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012) — pp. 66-69

name: Interventricular foramen
function: Paired communication between each lateral ventricle and the third ventricle, near the junction of frontal horn and body. The fornix bounds it anteriorly/superiorly and the anterior thalamic region posteriorly. Nearby choroid plexus and deep veins are important anatomical relationships; the opening is not a neural pathway.

efferent: Third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle

bloodSupply: The opening itself is not perfused tissue. Nearby thalamic/forniceal and plexal tissue has variable deep/choroidal arterial supply; deep veins are adjacent landmarks.

clinical.findings: A lesion near Monro can obstruct one or both lateral ventricles, sometimes causing intermittent or acute hydrocephalus. Sudden deterioration is possible but not the usual course of every small cyst.
One blocked foramen can produce predominantly ipsilateral lateral-ventricular enlargement; ventricular asymmetry alone does not prove obstruction.
A subependymal giant cell astrocytoma in tuberous sclerosis or another intraventricular mass may obstruct CSF flow. Imaging and disease context are needed for diagnosis.
